I know a fair bit of chemistry, and I know of nothing that can absorb salt and simply release it later.

Reverse osmosis and distillation work, but they use a lot of energy, which costs money. Reverse osmosis is basically a filtering system with molecule-sized pores that only water can pass through, but not the ions.

Ion exchange resins merely trade one ion for another. The trouble is that sodium and chloride are already the least troublesome ions. Trading the sodium chloride for iron bromide would make things worse.

I don't know of any materials that start with no ions and then grab a hold of sodium and chloride, and then easily release them later. There is no reason this is not possible, but it would take a lot of research to develop.

A better approach would be to use ice modifiers. Suppose each ice crystal was coated with a one molecule thick layer of a special protein. The protein would stick tightly to the ice but repel itself.
